里拉琴傳統上搭配故事或吟唱使用，古希臘游吟詩人常用以烘托氣氛。西北歐的日耳曼里拉: The lyre is traditionally used with a story or with singing, and the bards of ancient Greece often used it to set the mood. The Germanic lyre or rote of north-western Europe was used from before the Christian era into the Middle Ages, and in Scandinavia at least into the fourteenth century. It can still be heard in traditional music in Greece, Egypt, Ethiopia and elsewhere.
里拉琴共鳴箱通常採用烏龜殼或木材製作，頸部與臂架多為木製，常見選材為梧桐木或其他: The soundbox of the lyre is usually a tortoise shell or wood, and the neck and arms are mostly wood, commonly sycamore or another light wood. Historically the strings were made of sheep gut or ox tendon; modern strings are nylon or metal. Ivory or bone plates support and decorate the structure, and the tuning pegs are often wood or bone. The whole design is light so that it can be carried and played.
里拉琴屬弦鳴樂器，依 Hornbostel–Sachs 321.21-5 為魯特: The lyre is a chordophone and, by Hornbostel–Sachs 321.21-5, a yoke lute in the lute family: unlike other lutes, its strings are attached to two arms and a crossbar lying in the same plane as the soundboard. The soundbox is usually narrow so that it can be carried, which suits accompanying a story or a song. The box-bodied lyres of the east are wider, hold more strings, and have the soundhole in the back; the bowl lyre uses an open bottom as its soundhole. Plucking with the fingers and striking with a plectrum give a different contact and texture; the source gives no definite range or way of controlling volume.
里拉琴是古地中海弦鳴撥弦樂器，霍恩博斯特爾–薩克斯編號321.21-5，屬魯特琴: The lyre is an ancient Mediterranean plucked chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 321.21-5, a yoke lute of the lute family. Its strings are fixed to a yoke in the same plane as the soundboard, made of two arms and a crossbar, and the soundbox is narrow so that it can be carried. It is played with the fingers or a plectrum and often accompanies a story or singing; the bards of ancient Greece used it to set the mood, and it is also found in the traditions of Egypt, Ethiopia and elsewhere.
里拉琴有兩臂與橫樑，弦附於與共鳴面板同平面的軛上。薄型里拉以左腕腕帶支撐琴身，腕: The lyre has two arms and a crossbar, and the strings are attached to the yoke in the same plane as the soundboard. The thin lyre is supported by a wrist strap on the left wrist that runs to the bottom of the right arm, and the strings are struck with a plectrum; the thick lyre uses the fingers instead. The giant lyre is played standing, usually by two people. Beginners can start by learning the positions of the strings (usually five to eight, sometimes fifteen), holding the instrument steadily and sounding it with the fingers or a plectrum, and can accompany singing or narration.
里拉琴起源於古代地中海周邊文化，已知最早實物可追溯至約西元前2700年的美索不達: The lyre comes from the cultures around the ancient Mediterranean; the earliest known example dates from about 2700 BC in Mesopotamia. Early forms divide into the flat-based eastern lyre and the round-based western lyre: the first is found in Syria, Anatolia, the Levant and Egypt, while the second also comes from Syria and Anatolia, disappeared in the east around 1750 BC, reappeared in Greece around 1700 to 1400 BC, and spread with the Roman Empire. From it developed the Germanic lyre of Europe, used in the north-west from before the Christian era into the Middle Ages; medieval texts after the tenth century mostly use it allegorically, but in Scandinavia it lasted at least until the fourteenth century.
